1.open: Who taught you a skill you still use, and what do you remember about how they taught you?
questions: Paul calls Timothy "my true child in the faith" (v. 2). Who helped you in your faith, and what did they do that mattered?

Paul warns about people who devote themselves to "myths and endless genealogies" (v. 4) and who "turned aside to empty talk" (v. 6). What kinds of faith arguments tend to go in circles today, and why are they tempting?

Verse 5 says, "The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith." If love is the goal, how should that change the way we disagree with each other?
Paul says "the law is good, if one uses it legitimately" (v. 8). What does it look like to use something good in the wrong way?
Paul's list in verses 9 and 10 includes a few words whose exact meaning is debated, and Christians read them differently. How can we read a list like this honestly without turning it into a weapon?
Paul describes himself as "a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man," yet says "I was shown mercy" (v. 13). Why do you think he tells this part of his story so openly?

Verse 15 says, "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst." When you hear that, does it sound like good news, hard to believe, or something else? Answer as honestly as you can.
Paul urges Timothy to keep "holding on to faith and a good conscience" (v. 19), and warns that some have shipwrecked their faith. What helps you hold on when your faith feels shaky?
1.life: Write a short note or message this week to someone who helped you in your faith, and tell them one specific thing they did that mattered.
1.prayer: Thank God that "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" (v. 15), and that no one is out of reach. Ask for a heart that aims at love, especially when we disagree.
1.tip: Verse 10 contains a list with some debated words, and people in your group may hold strong views. Say in one sentence that Christians read it differently, then steer back to Paul's main point: the law restrains wrongdoing, mercy reached even him, and love is the goal. Invite anyone who wants to keep talking to do so after the meeting.

2.open: Who is someone you have prayed for, or been prayed for by, at a time when it really mattered?
questions: Paul begins by urging prayer "for everyone" (v. 1) and names "kings and all those in authority" (v. 2). Who is hardest for you to pray for, and what makes it hard?
Paul says the aim is that "we may lead tranquil and quiet lives" (v. 2). Why might a peaceful life matter for how the church shares its faith?

Verse 4 says God "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." Christians differ on whether "everyone" means every single person or people of every kind. What does this verse stir up in you either way?

Verse 5 says there is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Why do you think Paul stresses that Jesus is a man, and what does it mean to you that someone stands between you and God?
Verse 6 says Jesus "gave Himself as a ransom for all." If a ransom is the price paid to free someone, what do you think we needed freeing from?
Verse 8 asks for prayer "without anger or dissension." What does anger do to our prayers, and what does it take to set it down before we pray?
Verses 9 and 10 point to "good deeds" as the real adornment. How do people today, men and women, show off or hide behind appearance, and what would good deeds look like instead?

Verses 11 to 14 are among the most debated in the New Testament, and sincere Christians read them differently. If these verses leave you troubled, confused or unconvinced, what would you honestly say about that here?
2.life: Each day this week, pray by name for one person in authority, such as a local official, a boss or a school leader, especially one you disagree with. Ask God to bless them and to give them wisdom, without trying to fix them.
2.prayer: Thank God for Jesus, the one go-between who gave himself for all. Ask for a heart that wishes well for everyone, including people it is hard to pray for.
2.tip: Verses 11 to 15 will likely take over the evening. Say once, plainly, that faithful Christians disagree: some see a lasting rule, others a response to trouble in Ephesus. Then give most of your time to verses 1 to 8, and make sure no one is pressed to defend a position. For verse 15, it is fair to say scholars are unsure of its meaning, and no major Christian tradition teaches that women without children are shut out of salvation.

3.open: Think of someone you trusted with something important, like a key, a child or a secret. What made you trust them?
questions: Paul says that if anyone wants to lead, "he desires a noble task" (v. 1). How does that fit or clash with how people usually think about leadership?
Look at the list in verses 2 and 3. Which qualities are about character, and which are about skill? What do you notice about the balance?
Verse 2 says an overseer must be "able to teach," but most of the list is about temper, money, and how someone treats people. Why might Paul care so much about everyday habits?

Verse 5 asks, "how can he care for the church of God?" if he cannot manage his own household. What did Paul likely mean by that then, and how should we apply it carefully, given that no home is perfect?
Verses 8 to 10 say deacons "must first be tested." What are good, fair ways for a church to test someone before giving them responsibility, without making people feel judged?

Verse 11 can be read as being about deacons' wives or about women who served as deacons, and Christians differ on the roles in this chapter and how they apply today. How can we talk about that honestly and kindly, even if we land in different places?

Paul calls the church "the pillar and foundation of the truth" (v. 15). When have you seen a church hold truth up well, or seen it fall short? If you are unsure about church right now, what makes it hard?
Verse 16 tells of Jesus: "He appeared in the flesh," and was "believed in throughout the world." Which line stands out to you, and why might Paul end a list of leadership rules this way?
3.life: Pick one person who serves quietly in your church or community and thank them this week, in person or in writing. Then ask God to show you one small way you could serve.
3.prayer: Thank God for the people who lead and serve, and ask him to give them integrity and gentleness. Ask for help to see and grow in your own character, trusting his grace where you fall short.
3.tip: The marriage and household lines (vv. 2, 4, 12) can sting people who are single, divorced, or have struggling children. Name that early. Remind the group that Paul is describing what a trustworthy leader looks like, not ranking anyone's worth, and that Christians read these lines differently. Keep the focus on character and on the Jesus lines in verse 16.

4.open: What is something you have tried to get better at through regular practice, like a sport, an instrument or a skill, and what kept you going?
questions: Paul says some teachers will "prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods" (v. 3). Why might rules like these look holy from the outside?
Verse 4 says "every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected." What good gift from God do you tend to forget to thank him for?
Verse 2 describes people whose "consciences are seared with a hot iron." What do you think it looks like when someone stops feeling the wrong they do? How can we keep our own consciences tender?
Paul says "physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way" (v. 8). What would training in godliness look like in an ordinary week for you?

Verse 10 calls God "the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe." Christians understand this in different ways. What do you hear in it, and what does it say about God's heart for people?

Paul tells Timothy, "Let no one despise your youth" (v. 12), and to set an example in "speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." Which of those five is hardest for you right now, and who has shown it well to you?
Paul urges Timothy not to "neglect the gift that is in you" (v. 14). What do you think your gift or contribution might be, and what makes it hard to believe you have one?
If you feel unsure, tired or stuck in your faith, what is one honest thing you would say about where you are with the call to "persevere" in verse 16?
4.life: Pick one ordinary good gift this week, such as a meal, a friendship or a walk, and thank God for it out loud before you enjoy it. Then choose one small, steady habit of training, like reading a few verses each day, and keep it for the week.
4.prayer: Thank God for the good things he has made and ask him to help you receive them with gratitude. Pray for steadiness and for a growing faith that others can see.
4.tip: Verses 3 to 5 can drift into a debate about which foods or habits are allowed. Keep the group on Paul's point: the teachers made good things shameful, and Paul is not removing all self-discipline, since he urges training in verse 7. If someone feels guilty about their own discipline or lack of it, remind them that training grows over time and rests on God's grace.

5.open: Who has felt like family to you even though you are not related?
questions: Timothy is told to "appeal to him as to a father" when an older man needs correcting (v. 1). What changes in how we speak to someone when we treat them like family?
Verse 3 says, "Honor the widows who are truly widows." In that world a widow with no family had no income at all. Who is easy to overlook in our community today?
Verse 5 describes a widow who "puts her hope in God" when she is left all alone. Have you had a time when hope felt thin? What was that like, and what, if anything, kept you going?
Verse 8 says that anyone who does not provide for his own family "has denied the faith." Why might Paul use such strong words about everyday care for relatives?
Caring for family can be tiring, costly or complicated. What makes it hard, and what helps people keep going without burning out?

Paul warns that some younger widows may become "gossips and busybodies" (v. 13), and he advises them to marry and run households. Christians differ on how far this culture-shaped advice applies today. How do you separate what carries over from what belongs to that time?
Elders who lead well are "worthy of double honor" (v. 17), yet they are also to be corrected openly if they persist in sin (v. 20). Why does Paul want both respect and accountability for leaders?
Verse 25 says that even quiet good deeds "cannot remain hidden." Whose unnoticed kindness have you seen, and how could we thank them?
5.life: Think of one person who has little support, such as a widow, an older neighbor or a single parent. This week, do one practical thing for them, like a meal, a ride or an hour of help, and ask what they need.
5.prayer: Thank God for the people who have been family to you. Ask him to show you who needs care in your church and street, and to give your leaders wisdom and fairness.
5.tip: Verse 8 can sting people who are stretched thin or whose families are broken or unsafe. Say plainly that Paul is urging willing, practical care, not piling guilt on anyone, and that wise limits and the wider church's help both have a place.

6.open: What is something you bought or saved up for that you were sure would make you happy? Did it?
questions: Paul says, "godliness with contentment is great gain" (v. 6). What does contentment look like for you, and how is it different from simply giving up or not caring?
Verse 7 says, "we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it." How does it change the way you see your own belongings and plans?
Verse 8 says, "if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these." Where do you find that line hard to draw, between what you need and what you want?

Verse 10 says, "the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil." Paul points at the craving, not at money itself. What is the difference, and where have you seen that craving at work, in the world or in yourself?
Verse 5 describes people who "regard godliness as a means of gain." Why is it so easy to use faith for status, comfort or advantage, and how can a group guard against that?

In verse 11 Timothy is told to "flee" some things and "pursue" others, including "love, perseverance, and gentleness." Which of those do you most need to pursue right now, and what would a small step look like?
Verses 17 and 18 tell the rich to be "generous and ready to share." Compared with much of the world, most of us are rich. What would generosity look like in your life, even on a small budget?

Verses 1 and 2 on slaves and masters trouble many readers today, especially because they were once used to defend slavery. What questions or discomfort do these verses raise for you, and how might we read them honestly?
6.life: Pick one purchase or goal you have been chasing. Ask whether it is a need, a want, or a craving, and tell God honestly what you find. Then give something this week, money or time, to someone who needs it.
6.prayer: Thank God that he "richly provides all things for us to enjoy" (v. 17). Ask for a thankful heart that is content with enough, and for open hands to share what you have.
6.tip: Verses 1 and 2 may stir strong feelings, and the money verses may lead to guilt or comparing. Say plainly that these verses are troubling to many readers and were misused in the past, and let people voice that without rushing to explain it away. On money, Christians differ on whether Paul calls for a simple, modest lifestyle or mainly a right attitude and generosity. Do not settle it. Keep the focus on what each person can honestly take to God this week.
